etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hōm, from Old English hām, from Proto-West Germanic *haim, from Proto-Germanic *haimaz (“home, village”), from Proto-Indo-European *tḱóymos (“village, home”), from the root *tḱey-. Doublet of heyem.

definitions.definition: One’s own dwelling place; the house or structure in which one lives; especially the house in which one lives with one's family; the habitual abode of one’s family.

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, John xx:[10], folio clj, recto:
quote.text: And the diſciples went awaye agayne vnto their awne home.

quote.citation: 1808, John Dryden, edited by Walter Scott, The Works of John Dryden:
quote.text: Thither for ease and soft repose we come: / Home is the sacred refuge of our life; / Secured from all approaches, but a wife.

quote.citation: 1822, John Howard Payne, Home! Sweet Home!:
quote.text: Home! home! sweet, sweet home! / There’s no place like home, there’s no place like home.

quote.citation: 1981, William Irwin Thompson, The Time Falling Bodies Take to Light: Mythology, Sexuality and the Origins of Culture, London: Rider/Hutchinson & Co., page 132:
quote.text: If we now say that "woman's place is in the home," it is not because men put her there, but because the home became the capitol of women's mysteries.

quote.citation: 2013 June 29, “High and wet”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8842, page 28:
quote.text: Rock-filled torrents smashed vehicles and homes, burying victims under rubble and sludge.

definitions.definition: The place (residence, settlement, country, etc.), where a person was born and/or raised; childhood or parental home; home of one’s parents or guardian.

quote.citation: 2004, Jean Harrison, Home:
quote.text: The rights listed in the UNCRC cover all areas of children's lives such as their right to have a home and their right to be educated.

definitions.definition: The abiding place of the affections, especially of the domestic affections.

quote.citation: 1821, George Gordon Byron, Don Juan‎[1], canto III:
quote.text: He enter’d in the house—his home no more, / For without hearts there is no home; […]

definitions.definition: A house that has been made home-like, to suit the comfort of those who live there.
A place of refuge, rest or care; an asylum.
(by extension) The grave; the final rest; also, the native and eternal dwelling place of the soul.

quote.citation: 1769, King James Bible, Oxford Standard text, Ecclesiastes 12:5:
quote.text: […] because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets:  […]

definitions.definition: (by extension) Anything that serves the functions of a home, as comfort, safety, sense of belonging, etc.

quote.citation: 2007 January 10, Leslie Feinberg, “1976 WWP pamphlet found answers in Marxism”, in Workers World‎[2]:
quote.text: The rights of modern transsexual women and men to live in the sex that is "home".

definitions.definition: A dwelling.
One’s native land; the place or country in which one dwells; the place where one’s ancestors dwell or dwelt.

quote.citation: 1863, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Our Old Home: A Series of English Sketches‎[3]:
quote.text: Visiting these famous localities, and a great many others, I hope that I do not compromise my American patriotism by acknowledging that I was often conscious of a fervent hereditary attachment to the native soil of our forefathers, and felt it to be our own Old Home.

quote.citation: 1908, W[illiam] B[lair] M[orton] Ferguson, chapter IV, in Zollenstein, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: So this was my future home, I thought! Certainly it made a brave picture. I had seen similar ones fired-in on many a Heidelberg stein. Backed by towering hills, […] a sky of palest Gobelin flecked with fat, fleecy little clouds, it in truth looked a dear little city; the city of one's dreams.

quote.citation: 1980, Peter Allen, song, I Still Call Australia Home:
quote.text: I've been to cities that never close down / From New York to Rio and old London town / But no matter how far or how wide I roam / I still call Australia home.

definitions.definition: The locality where a thing is usually found, or was first found, or where it is naturally abundant; habitat; seat.

quote.citation: 1706, Matthew Prior, An Ode, Humbly Inscribed to the Queen, on the ẛucceẛs of Her Majeẛty's Arms, 1706, as republished in 1795, Robert Anderson (editor), The Works of the British Poets:
quote.text: […] Flandria, by plenty made the home of war, / Shall weep her crime, and bow to Charles r'estor'd, […]

quote.citation: 1849, Alfred Tennyson, In Memoriam A. H. H.:
quote.text: Her eyes are homes of silent prayer, / Nor other thought her mind admits / But, he was dead, and there he sits, / And he that brought him back is there.

quote.citation: 2013 September 7, “Nodding acquaintance”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8852:
quote.text: Africa is home to so many premier-league diseases (such as AIDS, childhood diarrhoea, malaria and tuberculosis) that those in lower divisions are easily ignored.

definitions.definition: (board games) The ultimate point aimed at in a progress; the goal.
(baseball) Home plate.
(lacrosse) The place of a player in front of an opponent’s goal; also, the player.
(Internet) The landing page of a website; the site's homepage.
(music, informal) The chord at which a melody starts and to which it can resolve.
A focus point.
(computing) Clipping of home directory.
(of animals, transitive) To return to its owner.
Of, from, or pertaining to one’s dwelling or country; domestic; not foreign. [from 13th c.]
(now rare, except in phrases) That strikes home; direct, pointed. [from 17th c.]
(obsolete) Personal, intimate. [17th–19th c.]

quote.citation: 1778, Frances Burney, Journals & Letters, Penguin, published 2001, page 91:
quote.text: I hardly knew what I answered him, but, by degrees I tranquillised, as I found he forbore distressing me any further, by such Home strokes […].

definitions.definition: (sports) Relating to the home team (the team at whose venue a game is played). [from 19th c.]
To one's place of residence or one's customary or official location.

quote.citation: 1863, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Our Old Home: A Series of English Sketches‎[4]:
quote.text: He made no complaint of his ill-fortune, but only repeated in a quiet voice, with a pathos of which he was himself evidently unconscious, "I want to get home to Ninety-second Street, Philadelphia."

quote.citation: 1892, Walter Besant, “Prologue: Who is Edmund Gray?”, in The Ivory Gate […], New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers, […], →OCLC, page 16:
quote.text: Athelstan Arundel walked home all the way, foaming and raging. No omnibus, cab, or conveyance ever built could contain a young man in such a rage. His mother lived at Pembridge Square, which is four good measured miles from Lincoln's Inn.

definitions.definition: To one's place of birth.
To the place where it belongs; to the end of a course; to the full length.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: Wear thy good rapier bare, and put it home:  […]

quote.citation: 1988, Roald Dahl, Matilda:
quote.text: Eventually she managed to slide the lid of the pencil-box right home and the newt was hers. Then, on second thoughts, she opened the lid just the tiniest fraction so that the creature could breathe.

definitions.definition: (Internet) To the home page.
To one's home.
At or in one's place of residence or one's customary or official location; at home.

quote.citation: 1975-1976, Lou Sullivan, personal diary, quoted in 2019, Ellis Martin, Zach Ozma (editors), We Both Laughed In Pleasure
quote.text: I'm certainly not the type to sit home waiting up for hubbie every night.

definitions.definition: To a full and intimate degree; to the heart of the matter; fully, directly.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis Bacon, dedication to the Duke of Buckingham, in Essays Civil and Moral,
quote.text: I do now publish my Essays; which of all my other works have been most current : for that, as it seems, they come home to men's business and bosoms.

quote.citation: 1692–1717, Robert South, Twelve Sermons Preached upon Several Occasions, volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London:
quote.text: How home the charge reaches us, has been made out by ẛhewing with what high impudence ẛome amongẛt us defend sin,  […]

quote.citation: 1748, [Samuel Richardson], “Letter LXVII”, in Clarissa. Or, The History of a Young Lady: […], volume (please specify |volume=I to VII), London:  […]  S[amuel] Richardson;  […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Her treatment of you, you say, does no credit either to her education or fine sense. Very home put, truly!

definitions.definition: (UK, soccer) into the goal

quote.citation: 2004, Tottenham 4-4 Leicester, BBC Sport: February,
quote.text: Walker was penalised for a picking up a Gerry Taggart backpass and from the resulting free-kick, Keane fired home after Johnnie Jackson's initial effort was blocked.

definitions.definition: (nautical) into the right, proper or stowed position
